title: Who ran it, and who owned it
lede: Roles are given as the sources describe them. Later careers are included only where we found a source.

people.name: Harry and Joseph Kaufman
people.text: The brothers founded Kaufman Brothers as a candy company in Pittsfield on April 1, 1922, and turned it toward toys during the Second World War.[^35]

people.name: Richard Kaufman
people.text: Harry’s son. He spent more than 35 years in the business and retired in the year Melville bought it. He died in October 2005, aged 82.[^35]

people.name: Howard Kaufman
people.text: He stayed for five years after the sale to Melville.[^26]
people.later: In 2012, aged 86, he told the Berkshire Eagle that “Bain paid the KB management a lot of money to stay in place, but the bulk of the company got nothing.”[^26]

people.name: William G. Kelley
people.text: He bought Kay-Bee in 1996 and in 1999 announced the web venture with BrainPlay.com.[^10] By the time of the sale to Bain, Michael Potter was Consolidated’s chairman and chief executive.[^14]

people.name: Michael Glazer
people.text: He led the management side of the 2000 buyout.[^14] Forbes reported that he received $18 million in the 2002 recapitalization.[^17] He was a defendant in the Big Lots suit that was dismissed in 2006.[^7]

people.name: Gregory Staley
people.text: A former president of the U.S. and international units of Toys “R” Us, he was named when KB left its first bankruptcy.[^21] The chief executive was replaced in the summer of 2007.[^22]

people.name: Andrew Bailen
people.text: A headquarters employee of 18 years told the Berkshire Eagle on the day of the layoffs: “Andy put his blood, sweat and tears into this place.”[^24]

people.name: Ellia Kassoff
people.text: He registered the KB Toys trademark in December 2016 and announced a revival in March 2018.[^30][^31]
people.later: In March 2019 he said the funding had not come together.[^33]
